\section[māne]{māne — the word already hiding inside "tomorrow," in four languages}

\label{lesson:LA-C31-mane}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You've already met this word once, without a lesson of its own — buried inside the very phrase that replaced \emph{crās} across half the Romance family. Time to meet it directly.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: māne — "morning," an indeclinable word}]
\textbf{Māne} — "\textbf{morning, early}" — is an \textbf{indeclinable} neuter noun (and adverb): unlike \emph{diēs} or \emph{nox}, it never changes its ending, no matter its grammatical role. You've already met it once, inside \textbf{dē māne} ("in the morning," Chapter 25) — the exact phrase that \textbf{French}'s \emph{demain}, \textbf{Italian}'s \emph{domani}, and \textbf{Catalan}'s \emph{demà} all independently rebuilt as their new word for "tomorrow," abandoning \emph{crās}. \textbf{Spanish}'s \emph{mañana} took a related but distinct path: built directly on \textbf{māne} itself, without the \emph{dē}- (Vulgar Latin \emph{*maneāna}) — the same root, one step closer to the source.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Māne traces to \textbf{mānus}, an archaic Latin adjective meaning "\textbf{good}." Watch the vowel length carefully: this is a \textbf{completely different} word from the everyday \textbf{manus} ("\textbf{hand}," short \emph{a}) — same spelling once macrons are dropped, unrelated meaning, a genuine false friend. From that "good" root comes \textbf{mātūrus} ("\textbf{ripe, timely, early}"), the direct source of English \textbf{mature} — and \textbf{mātūtīnus} ("of the morning," tied to \textbf{Matūta}, the Roman goddess of dawn), which gives English, via Old French \emph{matines}/\emph{matin}, both \textbf{matins} ("morning prayers") \textbf{and} \textbf{matinee} ("afternoon performance") — the same root splitting into two very different senses of "a scheduled morning-adjacent thing."
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}

  \item {[}YOU SAY: the false-friend warning — mānus "good" (long ā) vs. manus "hand" (short a){]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the English cousins — mature, matins, matinee, all from the same root as māne{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Where did you already meet \textbf{māne} before this lesson? (Inside \textbf{dē māne}, "in the morning," Chapter 25 — source of French \emph{demain}, Italian \emph{domani}, and Catalan \emph{demà}.) Did Spanish \emph{mañana} come from \emph{dē māne} too? (\textbf{Not quite} — it was built directly on \emph{māne} alone, without the \emph{dē}-.) Is māne's root \emph{mānus} the same word as \emph{manus}, "hand"? (\textbf{No} — a false friend; \emph{mānus} "good" has a long ā, \emph{manus} "hand" a short a.) What two very different English words both trace to māne's "good" root, via \emph{mātūtīnus}? (\textbf{Matins} and \textbf{matinee}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
